description_en: Originating in the 19th century CE, in 2019 Nāga Bāhāḥ Phalcā was rebuilt in "traditional" style from the ground up. The Nāga Bāhāḥ Phalcā was originally a one-storey structure, though unfortunately no historical photographs could be sourced. In 1980 (VS 2037), it was rebuilt in a two-storey configuration, albeit with no attention paid to maintaining a "traditional" appearance. It was built with regular brick in cement mortar, cement plaster, wood and steel shutters, plain windows and a corrugated metal roof cover.In 2019, Nāga Bāhāḥ Phalcā was dismantled and rebuilt again from ground up. For the foundation and base structure concrete and steel was used. According to a community member this was justified in order to make the Phalcā resistent against future earthquake damage. The upper structure follows traditional design parameters employing traditionaldāci apābrick, intricately carved pillars, finely decorated windows and a traditional timber-framed roof covered with hand-made terracotta tile (jhĩgaṭī)Śobhā Śākya, a member of the Province Parliament, provided the project with 49, 99,999 Nepali Rupees from the Parliamentary Fund.The upper floor is used as office space of Ṭola Sudhāra Simiti (Ṭola Development Committee).Traditionally, the open ground floor serves as a space for playing devotional music (bhajan).A serpent (nāga)paintingdecorates the ground floor wall, facing west. Local residents identify the serpent as Vāsukī, one of the four mythological serpent kings. The name of the locality, Nāga Bāhāḥ, is believed to be derived from the snake painting. Artists from the clan of Citrakāras of Taṅgala repaint the serpent every four years in preparation for thesamyakfestival. During this festival a peculiar ritual is performed: unhusked rice is poured through a hole in the ceiling onto the mouth of the serpent.A Buddha statue is installed in a niche in the north wall and a Gaṇeśa shrine is attached to the southern side of Nāga Bāhāḥ Phalcā.
description_ne: नागबाहाः स्थित हितिको (LAL0933) पूर्वतिर यो फल्चा अवस्थित छ । विसं २०३७ मा यो फल्चाको मौलिक रूप बिग्रने गरी सिमेन्ट र जस्तापाताको प्रयोग गरी पुनःनिर्माण गरिएको थियो । त्यो पुनःनिर्माणभन्दा पहिला फल्चा एक तलाको थियो भनिन्छ तर त्यस वेलाको फोटो उपलब्ध हुन सकेन । पुनःनिर्माणपछि फल्चाको माथिल्लो तलामा टोल सुधार समितिको कार्यालय र पुस्तकालय राखिएको थियो। फल्चामा बसेर भक्तजनहरू भजन गाउने गर्दथे ।फल्चाको भुइँतलाको पूर्वी भित्तामा नागको चित्र कोरिएको छ । उक्त नागलाई स्थानीयले वासुकि नाग मान्दै आएका छन् । यस नागको चित्रकै आधारमा समग्र बाहाःकै नाम नाग बाहाः रहन गएको मानिन्छ । प्रत्येक चार वर्षमा मनाइने सम्यक् पर्वमा नागको चित्रलाई तंगलका चित्रकार आई पुनःलेखन गर्ने परम्परा रहेको छ । सम्यक् पर्वको मध्याह्नको समय फल्चाको माथिल्लो तलामा धान थुपारिन्छ । उक्त धान सानो प्वालबाट भुइँतलामा झार्ने गरिन्छ । घण्टौँसम्म निरन्तर झर्ने धान भुइँतलाको नागको मुखनेर पर्ने गरी झार्नुपर्ने मान्यता रहेको छ ।सन् २०१९ जुनमा फल्चालाई पुनः मौलिक रूप दिन यसको पुनःनिर्माण कार्य सुरु गरिएको थियो। यसका लागि प्रदेश सरकारकी सांसद शोभा शाक्यको सांसद कोषबाट रू ४९,९९,९९९ उपलब्ध गराइएको थियो। पुरानो संरचना भत्काएर पुराना सबै निर्माण सामग्री फालिएको थियो । अहिले २०१९ अक्टोबरमा निर्माण सम्पन्न भएको छ । यसमा विभिन्न वास्तुशिल्पको प्रयोग गरिएको छ, तर पनि यसको मौलिक स्वरूपसँग मेल खाने खालको संरचना भने बने जस्तो देखिँदैन ।फल्चाको दक्षिणपट्टि गणेशको सानो देवल जोडिएर रहेको छ ।

historical_events.event_description: The Phalcā was renovated. It was plastered with cement and the roof was replaced with corrugated metal sheets.
Around VS 2040-2045 local youths established a library in the upper floor of the Phalcā. However, the library has been closed for many years as it was seldom used.

In June 2019, the Phalcāwas dismantled and all building materials were discarded. The reconstruction started in July 2019 and incorporated traditional design features. The painting of the snake was preserved and covered with a protective layer of foam. The foundations were rebuilt with reinforced cement concrete beams and the floor was recast as a 4-inch-thick steel reinforced concrete pad. The walls were constructed using modern brick withdāci āpāfacing. Six newly carved hard wood columns and highly decorated capitals and beams replaced the earlier plain timber frames. The first floor received a projecting central window and two flanking windows, all carved in great detail and vaguely resembling a late 19th century style.According to a local informant, the design for the Phalcā was provided by Rohit Ranjitkar from the KVPT. Working drawings were made by Anil Basukala.The project was conceptualised by Śobhā Śākya and funded through the Parliamentary Development Fund (Sāṃsada Vikāsa Koṣa/ सांसद विकास कोष).
